title: Police mum on fatal shooting details
article: --- The Saskatoon Police Service says the particulars of Friday's fatal shooting by an officer are not "within the public interest" so the force is keeping quiet until an inquest brings that information out.

"The minutia, the fine details of the event, I don't think it's within the public interest and as such, it's probably going to be withheld as being part of the investigation, pending review by the prosecution office," said police spokesperson Insp. Lorne Constantinoff. "The details in regard to this incident that have already been released by the department are as far as we're going. I think we've justified, as best as we possibly can, the actions of this officer."
A 10-year veteran constable, whose name is not being released by the police, shot a single bullet into the head of 35-year-old Andrew Wayne Moore shortly after 6:30 p.m. Friday.
Moore was well-known to the officer, who attempted to arrest him on outstanding warrants.
Moore fled and the constable gave chase into the Twenty-Ninth Street Confectionery and Grocery store in Westmount. The man, trapped inside the store, pulled out a handgun.
After about three warnings to drop the weapon, the officer was forced to shoot when the weapon was pointed in his direction, said Constantinoff, a use-of-force instructor for the police service.
The officer is off the job pending a psychological assessment. If he is cleared to return to work, he can do so while the investigation is underway.

Constantinoff would not say what type of gun Moore had, other than it was "a large-calibre handgun." "I do know (the calibre) but I'm not going to disclose that. And it's not necessarily that important either. It was a handgun and it was pointed in the vicinity of the officer, that's what's important," Constantinoff said.
He would also not comment on the struggle the officer and Moore had in the store, and when during the incident Moore's gun became evident.

"The minutia of the details is not something that we're to play out in the eyes of the media," he said. "There's going to be an inquest and the details are going to be relayed at that particular point. For us to sit here and debate back and forth and go into all of the details, this isn't the time or the place for it.

"I think what really justifies this particular shooting in the eyes of the police service is that this guy was armed, that he was holding a handgun, that he was pointing it in the vicinity of the officer and that he was refusing to drop it," Contantinoff said.

Constantinoff couldn't comment on whether Moore had a criminal record, saying it is not something the police department can disclose. Nor would he discuss the reasons behind the warrants -- for dangerous driving and obstructing a police officer -- that were issued against Moore in March by the same officer who shot him.
Another unanswered question is why the officer used pepper spray when, according to Chief Russell Sabo, Moore turned to walk away after first being told he was under arrest.

"The answer to these questions will end up raising more questions and then more questions and more questions. Pretty soon we're going to get to a point where we're going to be justifying it all again," Constantinoff said.
"That's what an inquest is all about. It will determine recommendations, how we can avoid situations like that, (and) whether or not the officer acted appropriately or didn't.

"This officer had previous dealings with this individual, he had a history with him. But I do not have details as to what constituted the warrants or what this officer's previous knowledge of this individual was."
Asked whether Moore was known to the force for criminal reasons or had connections to organized crime, Constantinoff could not say.
Moore was carrying a loaded firearm, which one can assume means he worried for his safety or was planning to be the aggressor in some instance, Constantinoff said.
"A person doesn't carry a gun just for the sake of carrying a gun. A person carries a gun for a purpose," he said. "You carry these things with intentions of using it."
Why Moore was the subject of this particular officer's attention, "I have no idea," said Constantinoff.
He did say the reason the officer called backup before approaching Moore is because the constable was alone at the time.

"There's safety in numbers as far as the police is concerned. Working by yourself and getting into a situation where you know you're going to have to place somebody under arrest, it's always wise to call back-up," Constantinoff said.
A toxicology report to indicate whether there were any drugs in Moore's system is likely to be done.
"That's standard for an autopsy," said Constantinoff.
Once the police service's major crimes division has done its internal investigation, the file will be forwarded to the Crown prosecutor's office for further recommendations.
